meta.title: Latin Phrases and Mottos
meta.subtitle: 625 phrases · both directions, as two cards per phrase
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Latin → English (see the phrase, recall what it means) and English → Latin (see the meaning, recall the phrase). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule. 625 Latin phrases, sayings and mottos — the well-known ones the Latin level decks leave, since those teach single words. WHERE THESE PHRASES COME FROM: English Wikipedia's List of Latin phrases, a curated list of some 2,400 rows, of which this deck keeps only the phrases with evidence that they are known beyond the list: 415 have a Wikipedia article of their own, and the others are entries in Wiktionary's Latin dictionary or quotations of three words or more found word for word in the classical authors (Caesar, Cicero, Livy, Virgil, Horace, Ovid and others). The phrases with an article come first, ordered by how often that article was read over two months of 2026, so carpe diem comes long before a phrase of canon law; the rest follow by how often they appear in the Tatoeba corpus and in the classical authors. Each card gives the phrase as the list spells it — without macrons, as Wikipedia prints Latin — with its translation and, where the list's note opens with a short sentence, that sentence: who said it, whose motto it is, how it is used. Example sentences from Tatoeba come with 177 of the 625 phrases, three apiece for 27, with the phrase picked out in colour. The speaker reads Latin with an Italian voice, which gives the Italianate church pronunciation, because almost no device has a Latin voice. Sources. Phrases, translations and notes: Wikipedia, List of Latin phrases (pages A to V, revisions of November 2026), CC BY-SA 4.0. Order: Wikipedia pageviews, September to November 2026. Selection: English Wiktionary via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0) and The Latin Library's texts of the classical authors. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
